title: A script that learns
objectives: Write a script that fits a line by nudging two weights until the error stops falling.

screens.title: Write what you did
screens.prose: You fitted the line by hand: start at (0, 0), do rounds, stop when a round changes nothing. A script can do the same.
screens.question: Put the script's steps in order.

lines.text: Set $w = 0$, $b = 0$ and the round count to 0
Do one round of nudging and add 1 to the count
If the round changed nothing, stop
Otherwise go back and do another round
Return $w$, $b$, the error and the count

hints.text: What has to happen before the first round?
Start, round, test, repeat, return.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The stopping test comes right after each round.

byKey.test: The test needs a round to have happened first.
byKey.ret: Returning comes only after the loop stops.

explain.text: The loop body is one round and a test. The test after each round is what stops the loop, as in first-python l6.

screens.title: The fitting script
screens.prose: Use `nudge_once` and `mse` (already written). Count every round, including the last one that changes nothing. Round $w$ and $b$ to 6 places at the end: 0.1 added fifteen times is `1.5000000000000002` in a computer, not exactly 1.5.
screens.question: Write `fit_by_nudging(xs, ys, step)` returning `(w, b, error, rounds)`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each list is accepted when every number is math.isclose to the expected one.

hints.text: Use `while True:` and `break` when nothing changed.
Inside: `new_w, new_b = nudge_once(w, b, xs, ys, step)`, then add 1 to `rounds`.
If `new_w == w and new_b == b`, break; otherwise set `w, b = new_w, new_b`.

feedback.correct: Your script fits the line and counts 16 rounds on the course data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Expected 16 rounds. If you got 15, count the last round, the one that changed nothing.
byKey.test-4: These points lie on $y = 0$, so the first round changes nothing: 1 round, $w = b = 0$.

explain.text:
The loop runs rounds and breaks on the first round that changes nothing.

```python
while True:
    new_w, new_b = nudge_once(w, b, xs, ys, step)
    rounds = rounds + 1
    if new_w == w and new_b == b:
        break
    w, b = new_w, new_b
```

screens.title: A coarser step
screens.prose: The script prints a line each round. Here is the start and the end of the run with step 0.1.
screens.question: With step 0.5 instead, how many rounds does `fit_by_nudging` count?

hints.text: Each round with step 0.5 can move $w$ and $b$ by 0.5.
Three rounds reach (1.5, 1.5).
The fourth round changes nothing: 4 rounds.

feedback.correct: Three moving rounds and one that changes nothing: 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the last round too.

byKey.moving: 3 rounds move the line. The fourth, which changes nothing, is counted too.

explain.text: With step 0.5 the line goes (0.5, 0.5), (1, 1), (1.5, 1.5), and a fourth round changes nothing: 4 rounds. It stops at MSE 0.1, coarser than step 0.1's 0.06.

params.title: Their loop
lines: new_w, new_b = nudge_once(w, b, xs, ys, step)

options.text: A test that stops the loop when a round changes nothing
A smaller step, so it reaches the end
options.why: Any step ends in a round that changes nothing. Without a test, the loop keeps going after that.

options.text: A counter of the rounds it has run
options.why: Counting is useful, but a counter alone does not stop anything.

options.text: A `return` line placed inside the loop
options.why: A `return` with no test would stop after one round.

hints.text: `while True` repeats until something breaks out.
Nothing here ever breaks out.

feedback.correct: Without a stopping test, `while True` never ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What would end a `while True` loop?

byKey.step: You changed the step. The loop still has no way to stop.

explain.text: `while True` runs until a `break`. The fix is the test you wrote: if the round changed nothing, break. Every loop needs a test that will become true (first-python l6).

screens.title: Ties that move
screens.prose: Another colleague keeps a nudge when it gives an **equal or lower** error, writing `<=` where we wrote `<`. Their points are (0, 1) and (0, 3): both have $x = 0$, so changing $w$ never changes the error.
screens.question: What happens when their script runs on these points?

options.text: A nudge keeps being accepted, so rounds can go on forever
Nothing changes: equal is as good as lower
options.why: With `<=` an equal error is accepted, so the line moves, and the round changed something.
Accepting ties can stop the rounds ever ending.
Nothing illegal happens; it just never stops.

hints.text: When does our script stop?
Only when a round changes nothing. With `<=`, a tie still changes something.

feedback.correct: Accepting ties lets the line wander forever without improving.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about when the stopping test can be true.

explain.text: Our loop stops when a round changes nothing. With `<=`, a nudge that only ties is accepted, so every round changes the line and the loop never ends. Strict `<` keeps a nudge only when the error really falls.

screens.title: Already perfect
screens.question: What does `fit_by_nudging(xs, ys, 0.1)` return as the round count?

hints.text: From (0, 0) the MSE is already 0.
The first round changes nothing, and it is counted.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The first round runs before the test.

byKey.zero: The test runs after a round, so at least one round is always counted.

explain.text: The MSE at (0, 0) is already 0, so no nudge can lower it. The first round changes nothing and the script stops, having counted 1 round.

screens.title: A script that reads its data
screens.prose: Make it a whole program: read five lines from the keyboard, each `x y`, fit with step 0.1 and print one line. For the course points it prints `w = 1.5, b = 1.3, error = 0.06`.
screens.question: Complete the script so it prints `w = ..., b = ..., error = ...` for any five points.

widget.how: Check runs your program 4 times, each with five input lines, and compares what it prints.

hints.text: `x, y = input().split()` reads one line into two pieces of text.
Turn each into a number with `float(...)` and append it to a list.
Then `w, b, error, rounds = fit_by_nudging(xs, ys, 0.1)` and print with an f-string.

feedback.correct: Your program reads, fits and prints.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare your printed line with the expected one.

explain.text:
Read five lines into two lists, fit, and print.

```python
for i in range(5):
    x, y = input().split()
    xs.append(float(x))
    ys.append(float(y))
```

screens.title: How every network learns
screens.prose: Your script did this: $$\text{change the numbers} \;\to\; \text{lower the error} \;\to\; \text{repeat until it cannot}$$ Every network in this strand learns that way, with millions of numbers instead of two. Later courses (`multivar` l8) find the downhill direction without trying both ways.
screens.question: What do a two-number line and a large network have in common?

options.text: Both change their numbers to lower an error on examples
Both follow rules a person wrote
options.why: The numbers are not written by a person; they are learned.

options.text: Both always reach the best possible numbers
options.why: Our rule stopped at 0.0608 with step 0.01, not the best. Stopping is not proof.

hints.text: What did your script do with $w$ and $b$?
It changed them to lower the MSE.

feedback.correct: Both lower an error by changing their numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the loop did.

explain.text: A model is a rule with numbers, and learning changes the numbers to lower an error on examples. Your nudging script is the smallest case.

screens.title: A line through prices
screens.prose: The same script fits a line to five days of a share's closing price against the day number. It prints `w = 0.22, b = 19.84`.
screens.question: What price does the line give for day 35, in pounds?

explain.text: The weight 0.22 means the line rises £0.22 a day, so day 35 gives $0.22 \times 35 + 19.84 = 27.54$. Trusting it is the l4 mistake: five days chose the line, and none of day 6 to day 35 tested it.

ideas: `fit_by_nudging` repeats rounds of nudging and stops on the first round that changes nothing; on our points it returns (1.5, 1.3, 0.06, 16).
A `while True` loop needs a test that breaks out; strict `<` makes every kept nudge lower the error.
Every network learns this way, by changing its numbers to lower an error on examples.

formula.name: The fitting loop
formula.note: Count every round, including the last.

summary.trap: A loop with no stopping test, or one that accepts ties, can run for ever.

quiz.prose: A nudging script moves the line in 7 rounds, then runs one round that changes nothing.
quiz.question: What round count does `fit_by_nudging` return?

feedback.correct: 7 moving rounds plus the round that changed nothing: 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count every round run.

byKey.moving: The final round, which changes nothing, is counted too.

explain.text: The script counts each round it runs, including the last. That is $7 + 1 = 8$.

quiz.question: Why does the script round `w` to 6 places?

options.text: Adding 0.1 many times leaves a tiny computer rounding error
The nudging rule made a mistake in a round
options.why: The rule landed on 1.5; the computer cannot store 0.1 exactly.

options.text: Six places is just tidier to print
options.why: It is tidier, but the reason is that 0.1 is not stored exactly.

feedback.correct: 0.1 is not stored exactly, so sums drift slightly.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how a computer stores 0.1.

explain.text: A computer stores 0.1 as a binary fraction that is very slightly off. Fifteen additions give `1.5000000000000002`. Rounding to 6 places removes the drift.

quiz.prose: A loop is written `while True:` with one round of nudging inside and no `break`.
quiz.question: What happens when it runs?

options.text: It does one round and stops
options.why: Nothing tells it to stop after one round.
Python runs it happily; it just never ends.

feedback.correct: Without a `break`, `while True` runs for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What would make `while True` stop?

explain.text: `while True` is always true, so only a `break` or `return` inside can end it. With neither, the loop never stops.
